title: feat(posit-dev): add new-work skill for todo tracking
description:
## Summary

Adds `/new-work`, a skill for creating and maintaining lightweight todo tracking documents in `_dev/todos/`. Each document captures status, context, plans, key files, and a decision log — enough that any fresh Claude Code session can resume work without re-explaining the problem.

The skill keeps the document updated throughout the session (decisions, commits, new discoveries) and points to `/working-on` for resuming in future sessions.

Also updates `/working-on` (v1.1) to write plans into the tracking document rather than only in chat.

Adds a Work Tracking Lifecycle section to `posit-dev/README.md` explaining how `/new-work`, `/working-on`, and `/implement` compose into a session-bridging workflow.

## Verification

Install the posit-dev plugin and start a new session in any repo:

```
/new-work
```

Claude should prompt for a todo location (or use `_dev/todos/` if it exists), create a date-prefixed markdown file in `pending/`, and keep it updated as work proceeds. At the start of a new session, `/working-on <path>` resumes tracking.

title: feat(shiny): add reactivity, testing, and agent-driving skills
description:
## Summary

Adds three Shiny skills to the `shiny` plugin, covering reactive design, testing, and agent-driven inspection — areas not yet covered by the existing `shiny-bslib` / `shiny-bslib-theming` skills.

- **`shiny-reactivity`** — design and debug Shiny's reactive graph in R: choosing between `reactive()`/`observe()`/`observeEvent()`/`eventReactive()`, managing state with `reactiveValues`, controlling execution with `req()`/`bindEvent()`/`bindCache()`/`debounce()`, and debugging with `reactlog`, tracebacks, and `profvis`. Leads with the observer-writes-state anti-pattern and the `bindCache()` key caveat.
- **`shiny-testing`** — the three testing layers (pure functions with `testthat`, reactive logic with `shiny::testServer()`, end-to-end with `shinytest2`/`AppDriver`) and guidance on what to test where, plus `exportTestValues()` and determinism practices.
- **`shiny-for-agents`** — drive and inspect a running app (R and Python) by waiting on Shiny's `shiny-busy` idle signal instead of sleeps, and read server-side errors the browser can't see. Frames `shinytest2`/`shiny.playwright` as the default for committed tests and live browser-driving as the fallback. Ships two helper scripts (`launch_app_dev.R`, `wait_for_shiny_idle.js`).

All three follow the repo's frontmatter conventions (`name`, `description`, `metadata.author`/`version`, `license: MIT`) and stay within the 5,000-token / 500-line `SKILL.md` and 100-token description limits — the largest is `shiny-for-agents` at ~2,317 tokens / 115 lines. Registered in `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` and documented in the root and `shiny/` READMEs.

## Verification

- `./count-skill-tokens.py shiny/<skill>` for each — all within limits, descriptions ~97–98 tokens.
- The load-bearing technical claims were validated empirically against R 4.6 / Shiny 1.13: `testServer` reading reactives and outputs; the `bindCache(input$x)` staleness caveat (stale on a `y`-only change, recomputes without the cache); `shinytest2::AppDriver` end-to-end (`set_inputs` auto-wait, `get_value(output=/export=)`, `wait_for_idle()` on a slow reactive); and — via chromote against the live app launched by `launch_app_dev.R` — that the `shiny-busy` class appears on `<html>` during server compute and clears at idle, plus `Shiny.shinyapp.isConnected()`/`$inputValues`.

title: feat(github): add issue-triage skill
description:
## Summary

Adds a new `issue-triage` skill under the `github/` category. Given a single GitHub issue, it finds genuine duplicates and clusters of related issues that could be fixed together in one multi-issue PR, then emits two text artifacts — a dedupe report and a multi-issue PR plan — for a human to act on. The skill is strictly read-only: it never comments, labels, closes, or pushes, which makes it safe for any repo member to run with only read access.

Design notes: context cost is bounded by the finalist set rather than repo size (server-side `gh search issues`, compact JSON fields, full bodies read only for ~5–8 finalists). A bundled `scripts/search-issues.sh` wraps `gh search issues` with the correct invocation, sidestepping two easy-to-miss gotchas (repo belongs in the `--repo` flag, not the query; `--state all` is invalid). The skill hands off to existing skills (`implement`, `pr-create`, `maintainer-decline`) for any write actions, and includes security boundaries treating issue content as untrusted data.

Registered in `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` under the `github` plugin and listed in `github/README.md`; the plugin/category descriptions were broadened from "pull request workflows" to "GitHub workflows" to cover triage.

## Verification

- `./count-skill-tokens.py github/issue-triage` → 168 lines / ~2,410 tokens (within the 500-line / 5,000-token limits); description ~50 tokens (under 100).
- End-to-end run against `rstudio/shiny#2144`: correctly identified duplicates (#3553, #4048, #3844) and a related issue (#3077), and produced both deliverables — all read-only.
- Helper script tested: multi-term search, `LIMIT` override, no-match (clean exit 0), missing args (exit 2); both documented `gh` gotchas reproduce when done the wrong way.

title: feat(posit-dev): add review-testing skill
description:
Adds a new `review-testing` skill to the `posit-dev` category.

## Summary
- Adds a skill that reviews test code for quality, design, and completeness after implementing a feature or fixing a bug. Activates on prompts like "review my tests", "are these tests good enough", and "check my test quality".
- The skill evaluates tests against four key qualities (regression protection, refactoring resilience, fast feedback, maintainability) across seven review areas: assertion completeness, test structure, fixture/state management, mocking boundaries, test smells (9 named patterns), naming/readability, and coverage gaps.
- Produces severity-tiered findings (Critical Issues → Required Changes → Strong Suggestions → Noted) with `file:line` references and concrete before/after examples. Offers to discuss, fix, or post findings as a PR comment.

## Verification
Trigger the skill in Claude Code after making changes that include test files:

```
/review-testing
```

or by asking Claude to "review my tests" or "are these tests good enough" after implementing a feature. The skill will find changed test files on the branch, trace back to the production code those tests cover, and produce a structured review with concrete findings.

## review-testing (157 lines, ~2,123 tokens)

> Review test code for quality, design, and completeness after implementing a feature or fixing a bug. Use when the user asks to "review my tests", "check my test quality", "are these tests good enough", "review testing", or after completing a feature implementation that includes tests. Also use when tests feel brittle, flaky, or superficial. Cross-references production code to find coverage gaps.

title: Add render-plan skill: markdown plans to Posit-themed HTML
description:
## Summary

- Adds a new `posit-dev/render-plan` skill that takes a markdown plan or spec file and produces a Posit-themed `.html` via Quarto.
- Applies the Posit style guide to the source `.md` automatically by chaining the existing `doc-reviewer` skill before rendering.
- Vendors `posit-dev/brand-yml/examples/brand-posit.yml` (with the `logo:` block removed since the placeholder logo filenames don't ship with brand-yml) so the skill works offline.

## Why

Plan and spec documents inside Claude Code sessions often need to leave Claude as a polished deliverable. Rendering through `quarto` + `_brand.yml` gives the right look out of the box; combining it with `doc-reviewer` produces a one-shot "make this plan presentable" command. The output is a single self-contained `.html` (via Quarto's `embed-resources`) — no sidecar `_files/` dir, no toolchain required on the recipient's side.

## How it works

1. Claude validates the input file and checks `quarto --version`. If Quarto is missing, the skill prints OS-specific install instructions and stops **before** touching the source.
2. Claude invokes `Skill("doc-reviewer")` against the source `.md`; edits are written in place.
3. Claude runs `scripts/render.sh`, which stages a temp workspace with the vendored `_brand.yml` and a generated `_quarto.yml` (with `embed-resources: true`), runs `quarto render`, moves the HTML next to the source, and opens it in the browser unless `--no-open` was passed.

## Test plan

- [x] Run `/render-plan path/to/plan.md` on a sample plan — HTML opens with Posit theming.
- [x] Run with `--no-open` — HTML is created but no browser opens.
- [x] Run with a non-existent path — non-zero exit, clear error.
- [x] Run on a system without Quarto — install instructions print, source is not modified.
- [x] Run on a style-guide-violating `.md` — source is edited in place by `doc-reviewer`.

title: refactor(quarto-authoring): make skill language-agnostic, add engines and jupyter refs
description:
## Changes

- Replace all `{r}` and `{python}` code cell examples with a `{language}` placeholder and pseudocode throughout the skill.
  Quarto's authoring layer (hashpipe options, cross-references, YAML metadata, layouts) is identical across all engines.
- Add `references/engines.md`: engine selection, auto-detection, hashpipe prefix per engine, and engine-specific behaviour differences (knitr auto-renders table objects; jupyter requires `output: asis` for portable markdown output).
- Add `references/conversion-jupyter.md`: bidirectional `quarto convert` (`.ipynb` ↔ `.qmd`) and format preference guidance.
- Add `output: asis` explainer to `references/code-cells.md`: what it does, requirements, and the `tbl-cap` caveat.
- Fix caching guidance in `references/code-cells.md` and `SKILL.md`: `#| cache: true` at cell level is knitr-only and is silently ignored by the jupyter and julia engines.
  Non-knitr engines use document-level `execute: cache: true` (requires `pip install jupyter-cache`).
  A blockquote warning makes this unambiguous at the top of the Caching section.
- Update SKILL.md description with fuller keyword surface (named engines, `.ipynb` trigger) to improve skill triggering coverage.
- DRY: `yaml-front-matter.md`, `code-cells.md`, and `conversion-jupyter.md` reference `engines.md` instead of repeating engine configuration content.
- Bump skill version to `1.4`, update Quarto CLI version note to `v1.9.36`.

## Benchmark

Three evals were run against the updated skill vs no skill (iteration 3):

| Eval | Topic | With skill | Without skill |
|------|-------|-----------|--------------|
| cache-regression | `cache: true` is knitr-only; jupyter uses `execute: cache: true` | 4/4 | 2/4 |
| julia-crossref | Cross-referencing Julia figures | 5/5 | 4/5 |
| output-asis | `output: asis` mechanics and `tbl-cap` caveat | 4/4 | 2/4 |
| **Overall** | | **100%** | **60%** |

The caching eval is the key regression test: without the skill, the model incorrectly recommends `#| cache: true` on Python cells (it is silently ignored); with the skill, it correctly directs users to document-level `execute: cache: true` and `pip install jupyter-cache`.

Supersedes #44

title: Add tidy-r skill for modern tidyverse R development
description:
## Purpose

This skill teaches Claude current tidyverse idioms. R syntax patterns have changed substantially since 2023, and Claude's defaults often lag behind. For example, it still reaches for `group_by() |> summarise() |> ungroup()` instead of `.by`, uses the deprecated `recode()`, and so forth. This skill corrects those habits. (NB: Supersedes #11. So this is a follow-up, even if unsolicited.)
 
## Use cases

- Writing or reviewing R code that uses dplyr, tidyr, stringr, or purrr.
- Migrating older tidyverse code to current patterns.
- Enforcing consistent style across a project.

## Testing

I installed the skill locally and verified that it activates on tidyverse-related prompts. Claude generally invokes the skill when writing R code by itself, though I would recommend to put an explicit pointer into CLAUDE.md. 

## Dependencies

None. This is a pure markdown skill with no external tools or packages required. There are some examples that suggest other packages (e.g., `tidylog`) but this is optional.

## Documentation

The main SKILL.md covers core rules and style conventions. Six reference files provide worked examples for grouping, joins, migration, recode/replace, stringr, and style. They are loaded only when the topic comes up.

## Token count

description:
## Summary

Reduces the quarto-authoring skill from ~37,172 to ~30,340 tokens (~18% reduction) across all 20 files while maintaining instructional quality.

Key changes:
- **Description** rewritten for activation matching (~99 tokens): uses user-facing language ("code cell options", "figure and table captions") instead of technical shorthand ("hashpipe", "divs/spans")

- **markdown-linting.md** rewritten to cover only Quarto-specific allowances (MD013, MD024, MD025, MD033, MD041) and config — standard markdownlint rules removed since any LLM already knows them
- **callouts.md** consolidated: 5 identical type examples replaced with 1 + type list; Complex Content and trailing Examples sections removed
- **All conversion guides** (rmarkdown, bookdown, xaringan, distill, blogdown): duplicated step-by-step sections removed since they restate Quick Start + detailed sections above them
- **All 19 reference files**: `## Resources` sections preserved with quarto.org links (useful for LLMs to fetch authoritative docs)
- **Remaining files**: verbose multi-example blocks condensed where standard syntax (Mermaid diagram types, HTML tables, Graphviz examples) was shown 3+ times

description:
## Purpose
This skill provides guidance on modern tidyverse patterns, style conventions, and migration paths for R development. It helps Claude write idiomatic tidyverse code following current best practices (R 4.5+, tidyverse 2.0+).

## Use cases
- Writing new R code using tidyverse packages
- Reviewing tidyverse code for style consistency
- Updating legacy R code to modern patterns (base R → tidyverse, old tidyverse → new)
- Enforcing consistent style across a project

## Testing
- Tested with Claude Code using the R (btw) MCP server
- Verified skill activates when writing/reviewing R code
- Tested migration suggestions from legacy patterns

## Dependencies
- Works best with the [R (btw) MCP server](https://github.com/posit-dev/btw) for automatic function documentation lookup (optional)

## Documentation
- Main SKILL.md covers core patterns with inline examples
- Reference files in \`references/\` provide detailed examples:
  - \`join-examples.md\` - join_by() patterns
  - \`grouping-examples.md\` - .by, pick(), across(), reframe()
  - \`stringr-examples.md\` - string manipulation
  - \`migration-examples.md\` - legacy → modern conversions
  - \`tidyverse-style.md\` - style guide summary

## Inspiration
- https://gist.github.com/sj-io/3828d64d0969f2a0f05297e59e6c15ad
- https://github.com/jeremy-allen/claude-skills"

title: chore: No `README.md` files next to `SKILL.md` files
description:
From the skill-creator skill:

>   A skill should only contain essential files that directly support its functionality. Do NOT create extraneous documentation or auxiliary files, including:
> 
>   - README.md
>   - INSTALLATION_GUIDE.md
>   - QUICK_REFERENCE.md
>   - CHANGELOG.md
>   - etc.
> 
>   The skill should only contain the information needed for an AI agent to do the job at hand. It should not contain auxilary context about the process that went into creating it, setup and testing procedures, user-facing documentation, etc. Creating additional documentation files just adds clutter and confusion.

title: Add a create-release-checklist skill for R packages.
description:
This commit introduces a skill to create Tidyverse-style release checklist issues for R packages, similar to using
`usethis::use_release_issue()`.

There are some interesting advantages to doing this with the help of an agent:

- It's surprisingly good at automating stuff like picking an appropriate version bump.
- It's nice to have the option to say things like "we don't need a blog post or social media announcement for this package" and have it excise the corresponding tasks.

Finally, note that the "pure R" way of doing this would be to use the `gh` package for GitHub operations, but since we're in the terminal here anyway I find the official `gh` CLI just much more powerful, and Claude is very good at troubleshooting with it.
